prompt: On a dot plot, what does each dot stand for?

options.text: One value, such as one student's answer
The mean of the data
The total for a whole category
The time the data was collected

feedback.b: A dot plot shows every value. You can work out the mean from it, but no single dot is the mean.
feedback.c: That describes a bar in a bar graph. On a dot plot, you count the dots to get a total.
feedback.d: Time-series graphs show data over time. A dot plot shows one dot per value.

hints: Think about what you count when you read a dot plot.
solution: Each dot stands for **one value**: one student, one game, one measurement. Dots with the same value stack on top of each other.

prompt: Match each display to the data it suits best.

right.text: How a value changes over time
One numerical variable, with one dot per value
Two categorical variables, with bars side by side
One categorical variable, with one bar per category

hints: "Clustered" means grouped together.
solution: Time-series graph: change over time. Dot plot: one numerical variable. Clustered bar graph: comparing two categorical variables. Bar graph: one categorical variable.

prompt: Select **all** the things that help make a good graph.

options.text: A title that says what the graph shows
Axis labels, with units if needed
A scale that goes up in equal steps
Saying who the data came from
Bright 3D effects
Leaving out the numbers on the axis to keep it tidy

hints: Which features help someone read the graph accurately and know what it is about?
solution: A good graph has a **title**, **axis labels** (with units), an **even scale** and a note of **who the data came from**. 3D effects make bars harder to compare, and a graph with no numbers on the axis can't be read.

prompt: Which of these is a **statistical question**?

options.text: How many hours of sleep do Year 7 students at our school usually get?
How many hours did I sleep last night?
How many hours are in a day?
What time does the school bus leave?

feedback.b: This has just one answer, so you don't need to collect data from lots of people.
feedback.c: This is a fact: there are always 24 hours in a day.
feedback.d: This is a fact you can look up on the timetable.

hints: A statistical question needs data, and the answers vary.
solution: To answer "How many hours of sleep do Year 7 students usually get?" you need to collect data from many students, and their answers will vary. So it is a **statistical question**.

prompt: Mia measured the temperature outside her classroom every hour from 9 am to 3 pm. Which display should she use?

options.text: A time-series graph
A dot plot
A clustered bar graph
A stacked bar graph

feedback.b: A dot plot would show the temperatures, but not when each one happened.
feedback.c: Clustered bar graphs compare two categorical variables.
feedback.d: Stacked bar graphs compare two categorical variables.

hints: The data was collected over time.
solution: The temperature was measured **over time**, so a **time-series graph** is best. It shows how the temperature changed during the day.

prompt: Give a possible reason for the outlier. Should Tama remove it from his data? Explain.
modelAnswer: The student might live a long way from school, for example on a farm, or might walk a long way round to pick up a younger sibling. Tama should check that the value was recorded correctly. If it is real, he should keep it, because an outlier isn't necessarily a mistake. He could mention it when he describes the data.

rubric.criterion: Gives a sensible real-life reason for a 25-minute trip, such as living further away
Says to check the value and keep it if it is real, because outliers aren't always mistakes

hints: Why might one student take much longer than the others?
Are outliers always mistakes?
solution: A real reason could be that the student lives much further away. Outliers are not always errors, so Tama should check the value and keep it if it is correct.

prompt: Put the steps of a statistical investigation in order.

items.text: Plan what data to collect and how
Collect the data and record it in a table
Display the data in a suitable graph
Describe what the graph shows and answer the question

hints: You need a question before you can plan, and data before you can draw a graph.
solution: Question → plan → collect → display → describe and answer. Each step depends on the one before it.

prompt: Ruby wants to compare how Year 7 and Year 8 students get to school. Which display is best?

options.text: A clustered bar graph
A dot plot
A time-series graph
A bar graph of the Year 7 students only

feedback.b: A dot plot shows one variable. Here there are two categorical variables to compare.
feedback.c: The data isn't collected over time.
feedback.d: Then she couldn't compare the two year groups at all.

hints: How many variables are there? Are they categorical or numerical?
solution: There are two categorical variables: way of getting to school, and year group. A **clustered bar graph** puts the Year 7 and Year 8 bars side by side, so they are easy to compare. (A stacked bar graph would also work.)

prompt: Ella is drawing a bar graph. Her biggest value is 38. Her vertical scale starts at 0 and goes up in steps of 5. What is the smallest number the top of her scale can be, so that every bar fits?
hints: The scale goes 0, 5, 10, 15, …
Which number in that list is the first one that is at least 38?
solution: The scale goes 0, 5, 10, …, 35, 40. 35 is too small for a bar of 38, so the top of the scale must be at least **40**.

solution:
The Year 8 bar reaches 20, so there are 20 Year 8 students. The rugby part goes from 0 to 10, so 10 chose rugby.

prompt: Hana's dot plot of how long students slept last night has one dot at 3 hours. All the other dots are between 8 and 11 hours. What should Hana do?

options.text: Check that the value is correct, and keep it if it is real
Delete it, because outliers are always mistakes
Change it to 9 hours so it fits with the rest
Throw away the whole data set

feedback.b: Outliers aren't always mistakes. That student might really have had a bad night.
feedback.c: Changing data to make it fit would make the results untrue.
feedback.d: One unusual value doesn't spoil the rest of the data.

hints: Are outliers always mistakes?
solution: 3 hours is an **outlier**. It might be a recording mistake, or a student might really have slept badly. Hana should check it and keep it if it is real. She can mention it when she describes the data.
